purpose: Thioguanine is a chemotherapy medicine mainly used to treat certain types of leukemia, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It is sometimes used alone or combined with other cancer medicines to help slow or stop the growth of cancer cells. Your doctor has chosen this medicine as part of your cancer treatment plan.
how_it_works: Thioguanine works by pretending to be a natural building block that your body uses to make DNA. Cancer cells mistakenly use it instead of the real building block, which causes errors in their DNA and eventually kills them. Because cancer cells grow and divide much faster than most normal cells, they are hit hardest by this medicine.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite are common, especially early on. You may notice mouth sores, diarrhea, or a drop in your blood counts, which can make you feel tired or more prone to infections or bruising. Skin rash and hair thinning can also occur.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your blood cell counts, raising your risk of serious infections, bleeding, or anemia — your doctor will monitor your blood regularly. Long-term use can cause liver damage, including a serious condition called veno-occlusive disease, so any yellowing of skin or eyes, belly pain, or swelling should be reported immediately. This medicine can harm an unborn baby, so effective contraception is very important during treatment. Never take this medicine without close medical supervision.
typical_dosing: The dose is carefully calculated based on your body weight or body surface area and the specific condition being treated. A typical starting dose is around 2 mg per kilogram of body weight taken by mouth once daily, but your doctor will set the exact dose that is right for you. Always follow your doctor's instructions precisely and never adjust your dose on your own.
